pages.text: Pip is a pup.
Pip has a red ball.
Pip kicks the ball.
The ball rolls and rolls.
Where is the ball?
Pip can not see it.
A cat sits on a log.
The cat sees the ball in a bush.
Pip gets the ball.
Pip and the cat play all day.

gloss: pup. pup means a baby dog.
bush. bush means a small, round plant with lots of leaves.
log. log means a big, fallen piece of a tree.

qs.q: What did Pip lose?
Who found the ball?
How does Pip feel at the end?

books.title: Pip and the Red Ball

pages.text: Mia has a tiny seed.
She digs a hole in the soil.
Mia drops the seed in the hole.
She pats the soil on top.
Rain falls on the soil.
Then the sun comes out to warm it.
One day, a green sprout pops up!
Mia jumps up and down.
Soon the sprout is a big sunflower.
It is taller than Mia!

gloss: soil. soil means dirt where plants grow.
sprout. sprout means a new little plant.
taller. taller means more tall; higher up.

qs.q: What did Mia do first?
What helped the seed grow?
Why did Mia jump up and down?
o: She was excited to see the sprout

books.title: Mia's Tiny Seed

pages.text: It is a windy day.
Sam has a new kite.
Sam runs fast.
The kite goes up, up, up!
Oh no!
The wind stops.
The kite falls down.
Dad sits with Sam.
They wait for the wind.
Whoosh!
The wind is back.
The kite flies high in the sky.

gloss: windy. windy means when lots of wind is blowing.
whoosh. whoosh means the sound of fast wind.

qs.q: Why did the kite fall down?
What did Sam and Dad do?
The word whoosh is the sound of…

books.title: Sam's Windy Day

pages.text: Ama and her grandmother walked along the beach after sunset.
Grandma carried a small flashlight, and Ama carried a big question: would they see the turtles tonight?
Near the dunes, the sand began to wiggle.
Tiny flippers poked out, one after another.
Baby sea turtles! Ama whispered.
She lifted her flashlight to see them better.
Grandma gently pushed the light down.
Turn it off, she said softly.
Bright lights confuse the babies. They follow the moon to find the sea.
Ama switched off the light.
In the silver moonlight, the hatchlings scrambled toward the waves.
The last little turtle reached the water and swam away.
Ama squeezed Grandma's hand.
I'm glad we helped, she said.

gloss: dunes. dunes means hills of sand near a beach.
hatchlings. hatchlings means baby animals that just came out of their eggs.
confuse. confuse means to mix someone up so they do not know what to do.
scrambled. scrambled means moved quickly using hands and feet.
flippers. flippers means flat legs that help an animal swim.

qs.q: What is this story mostly about?
o: Ama learns how to help baby turtles reach the sea

qs.q: Why did Grandma ask Ama to turn off the light?
o: Bright lights confuse the baby turtles
It was time to go home

qs.q: In this story, hatchlings are…
o: Baby turtles that just came out of their eggs

qs.q: How does Ama feel at the end?

books.title: Ama and the Moonlight Turtles

pages.text: Kofi wanted to play the drum at the school festival.
There was just one problem: his rhythm kept falling apart.
Every afternoon, he practiced on an old paint bucket in the backyard.
His dog, Biscuit, howled along.
Some days his hands hurt, and he wanted to quit.
Then he remembered his uncle's advice: Slow is smooth, and smooth becomes fast.
So Kofi slowed down.
He counted every beat out loud: one, two, three, four.
On festival day, the crowd clapped along to his steady beat.
Even Biscuit wagged his tail in time.

gloss: rhythm. rhythm means a pattern of beats in music.
festival. festival means a big celebration with music and food.
steady. steady means not changing; even and regular.
advice. advice means an idea that helps someone decide what to do.

qs.q: What lesson does this story teach?
o: Practicing patiently helps you get better

qs.q: What did Kofi practice on?
What does Slow is smooth, and smooth becomes fast mean?
o: Do it slowly and correctly first, and speed will come

qs.q: What did Kofi do right after he remembered the advice?
o: He slowed down and counted the beats

books.title: Kofi's Steady Beat

pages.text: A honeybee can visit hundreds of flowers in a single day.
It is looking for nectar, a sweet liquid inside each flower.
The bee sips the nectar and stores it in a special stomach called a honey stomach.
Then it flies back to the hive.
Inside the hive, the bee passes the nectar to another bee.
The bees chew it and add enzymes, which slowly change it.
Next, the bees spread the nectar into wax cells.
They fan their wings to dry it until it becomes thick, sticky honey.
Finally, the bees seal each cell with a wax cap.
The honey will feed the whole colony through the winter.

gloss: nectar. nectar means a sweet liquid inside flowers.
hive. hive means the home where a group of bees lives.
enzymes. enzymes means natural helpers that change one thing into another.
colony. colony means a big group of bees that live together.
cells. cells means small six-sided rooms made of wax.

qs.q: How is this text organized?
o: As a problem and a solution

qs.q: What is nectar?
o: The wax cap on a cell

qs.q: Why do bees fan their wings?
o: To dry the nectar so it becomes honey

qs.q: What is the main idea?
o: Bees turn nectar into honey in several steps

books.title: How Bees Make Honey

pages.text: On Moon Base Nine, twelve-year-old Zara knew every hum and beep of the habitat.
So when the hallway lights flickered and the air fans went quiet, she noticed before the alarms did.
Power is dropping, Commander Osei announced over the speaker.
Everyone report to the central dome.
His voice was calm, but Zara saw her mother grip the railing.
On the main screen, the numbers told the story: the solar panels were making only a third of their usual power.
Yet the sun was shining directly on them.
Zara remembered the dust storm from two days earlier.
Moon dust is sharp and clingy; it sticks to almost everything.
What if the panels aren't broken, she said slowly, just dirty?
The commander sent a rover with a soft brush arm.
Panel by panel, it swept away the gray film.
With each pass, the power reading on the screen climbed higher.
When the fans whirred back to life, the crew cheered.
Commander Osei shook Zara's hand.
Good scientists ask simple questions first, he said.

gloss: habitat. habitat means a place where people or animals live; here, the moon base.
flickered. flickered means went quickly on and off.
rover. rover means a vehicle that drives over rough ground.
film. film means a very thin layer covering something.

qs.q: What was really causing the power problem?
o: Moon dust covered the solar panels

qs.q: Zara saw her mother grip the railing. What does this detail show?
Which clue helped Zara figure out the panels might be dirty?
o: A dust storm had happened two days earlier

qs.q: What does Good scientists ask simple questions first mean?
o: Check the easiest explanation before the hard ones

books.title: The Dusty Panels of Moon Base Nine

pages.text: Many middle schools start before eight o'clock in the morning.
Some researchers and doctors argue that this schedule works against how young teenagers' bodies are built.
During the early teen years, the body's internal clock shifts.
Many young people do not feel sleepy until later at night, which makes early wake-up times hard.
Supporters of later start times point to schools that changed their schedules.
In several of these districts, students slept longer and attendance improved.
Others disagree.
They say later start times can make bus routes more expensive, push after-school sports into the evening, and complicate family schedules.
Both sides want students to succeed.
The real question is which costs a community is willing to accept, and which benefits matter most.

gloss: researchers. researchers means people who study a topic carefully to learn facts.
internal. internal means inside; your body’s own.
districts. districts means groups of schools in one area.
complicate. complicate means to make something harder or more confusing.

qs.q: What is the author's main purpose?
o: To explain both sides of a debate
To convince readers schools must start later
To tell a funny story about a bus

qs.q: Which detail supports the idea that later start times can help?
o: Students slept longer and attendance improved

qs.q: What is one reason some people disagree with later start times?
o: Bus routes could become more expensive

qs.q: In this text, an internal clock is…
o: Your body's natural sense of when to sleep and wake
A clock on the school wall

books.title: Should School Start Later?

pages.text: Long ago, Kwaku Anansi the spider decided that he would gather all the wisdom in the world.
He went from village to village, scooping every clever idea into a clay pot.
When the pot was full, Anansi began to worry.
If anyone finds this, they will become as wise as I am, he thought.
So he decided to hide it at the top of the tallest tree in the forest.
He tied the heavy pot to the front of his body and began to climb.
But the pot bumped against the trunk with every step, and he kept sliding back down.
His young son, Ntikuma, had been watching from below.
Father, he called, why not tie the pot on your back? Then you could hold on to the tree.
Anansi stopped.
His son, who had none of the pot's wisdom, had solved the problem in a moment.
Anansi realized he had never truly held all the wisdom in the world.
Frustrated, he let the pot slip.
It crashed to the ground, and the wisdom scattered on the wind.
That is why, the story says, a little wisdom can be found in everyone.

gloss: wisdom. wisdom means good sense and knowledge about how to live and solve problems.
gather. gather means to collect things into one place.
frustrated. frustrated means upset because something is not working.
scattered. scattered means spread out in many directions.

qs.q: What is the lesson of this folktale?
o: No one has all the wisdom; everyone has some

qs.q: What is surprising, or ironic, about how the problem gets solved?
o: The son with none of the pot's wisdom solves it

qs.q: Why did Anansi want to hide the pot?
o: So no one else would become as wise as he was
To keep it dry from the rain
To give it to his son later

qs.q: This folktale explains why something is the way it is. What does it explain?
o: Why a little wisdom can be found in everyone

books.title: Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom

pages.text: Kofi lives in Ghana.
His grandpa makes kente cloth.
Grandpa weaves gold, then green.
Gold, green, gold, green.
What comes next? asks Grandpa.
Gold! says Kofi.
Kofi wants to make a strip too.
He picks red, blue, red, blue.
Kofi gives the strip to Mama.
Mama wears it with pride.

gloss: weaves. weaves means makes cloth by crossing threads over and under.
strip. strip means a long, thin piece.
pride. pride means a happy feeling about something good.

qs.q: What does Grandpa make?
Gold, green, gold, green. What comes next?
How does Mama feel about the strip?

books.title: Kofi's Kente Colors

pages.text: It rained all night.
In the morning, Ben saw a big puddle.
Ben jumped in the puddle.
Splash!
The sun came out.
It was hot all day.
After lunch, the puddle was small.
By night, it was gone!
Where did it go? Ben asked.
The sun turned it into water vapor, said Mom.
The water went up into the air, said Mom.
Someday it will rain down again!

gloss: puddle. puddle means a small pool of water on the ground.
vapor. vapor means water that has turned into a gas in the air.

qs.q: What happened FIRST?
What made the puddle go away?
Where did the water go?

books.title: Where Did the Puddle Go?

pages.text: Nia went to the library with Dad.
She wanted her very own library card.
Nia wrote her name on a form.
She printed each letter with care.
The librarian gave Nia a blue card.
You can borrow three books, she said.
Nia picked a book about frogs, one about stars, and one about trucks.
At home, Nia read to her baby brother.
He clapped at every picture.
I will bring them back next week, Nia said.
Then I can borrow three more!

gloss: librarian. librarian means a person who helps people find books.
borrow. borrow means to take something and give it back later.
form. form means a paper you fill in.

qs.q: How many books can Nia borrow?
Which book did Nia NOT pick?
Why will Nia bring the books back?
o: Because she did not like them

books.title: Nia's First Library Card

pages.text: Every Saturday, Akosua helps her aunt sell fruit at Makola Market in Accra, Ghana.
The market is loud, busy and full of color.
Auntie Esi sells pineapples for 10 cedis each and mangoes for 5 cedis each.
Cedis are the money used in Ghana.
A woman asked for two pineapples and one mango.
Akosua added in her head: ten plus ten plus five.
That will be 25 cedis, she said.
The woman handed her a 50-cedi note.
Akosua counted up from 25, one note at a time, until she reached 50.
Here is your change: 25 cedis, Akosua said, smiling.
Auntie Esi raised her eyebrows.
Who taught you to count change so fast?
You did, Akosua laughed, every Saturday!

gloss: cedis. cedis means the money used in Ghana.
change. change means money you get back when you pay more than the price.

qs.q: How much does one pineapple cost?
Why did the woman owe 25 cedis?
o: Two pineapples and one mango cost 10 + 10 + 5

qs.q: How much change did the woman get?
What does Akosua's answer You did show?
o: She learned by practicing with her aunt each week
She went to a math school

books.title: Akosua's Market Day

pages.text: In 1781, the American Revolution was still being fought in Virginia.
James Armistead was an enslaved man who lived in New Kent County.
James wanted to help the Americans win.
He asked to serve with the Marquis de Lafayette, a French general helping the American army.
Lafayette sent James to the British camp as a spy.
The British thought James was working for them.
James listened carefully.
He sent secret reports about British plans back to Lafayette.
His reports helped the Americans and the French trap the British army at Yorktown.
In October 1781, the British surrendered.
After the war, James was still enslaved.
Lafayette wrote a letter praising his work, and in 1787 Virginia granted James his freedom.
He took the name James Armistead Lafayette.

gloss: spy. spy means a person who secretly gathers information.
reports. reports means information that is told or written down.

qs.q: Where was the British army trapped?
Why did the British talk about their plans near James?
o: They thought he was working for them

qs.q: What was one result of James's reports?
o: The British army was trapped and surrendered

qs.q: How did James gain his freedom?
o: Virginia granted it in 1787 after Lafayette praised him

books.title: The Spy Who Helped Win Yorktown

pages.text: Maya was the fastest player on the Tornadoes, her soccer team.
But the Tornadoes had lost three games in a row.
Every time Maya got the ball, she tried to score by herself.
Every time, three defenders surrounded her.
After practice, Coach Rivera drew circles on a whiteboard.
Soccer is like a spider web, she said.
It is strongest when every strand is connected.
In the next game, Maya saw Jada open on the left.
She passed instead of shooting.
Jada kicked the ball into the corner of the net.
The Tornadoes cheered louder than they had all season.
They still did not win every game after that.
But they never lost three in a row again.

gloss: defenders. defenders means players who try to stop the other team from scoring.
strand. strand means one thin thread.
surrounded. surrounded means all around on every side.

qs.q: What was the team's problem at the start?
o: They had lost three games in a row

qs.q: What did Coach Rivera mean by the spider web?
o: The team is strongest when players work together

qs.q: How did Maya change?
What is the theme of the story?

books.title: Team Tornado

pages.text: Bakari had never seen so much sand.
For twenty days, his uncle's camel caravan had crossed the Sahara, carrying slabs of salt from the mines of Taghaza.
In Timbuktu, salt is worth almost as much as gold, Uncle Moussa said.
People need it to keep food from spoiling and to stay healthy in the heat.
When the walls of Timbuktu finally appeared, Bakari gasped.
Traders filled the market, trading salt for gold, cloth and ivory.
But what amazed Bakari most were the scholars.
In the shade of the great mosque, students copied books by hand and argued about mathematics, medicine and the stars.
Under Mansa Musa, Mali grew rich from trade, a scholar told him.
But our greatest treasure is knowledge, because it cannot be stolen.
On the long journey home, Bakari carried something new: a small book his uncle had traded for.
He decided he would learn to read every page.

gloss: caravan. caravan means a group of traders traveling together, often with camels.
slabs. slabs means thick, flat pieces.
scholars. scholars means people who study and know a great deal.

qs.q: What did the caravan carry to Timbuktu?
Why was salt so valuable?
o: People needed it to keep food from spoiling and to stay healthy
It was used to build houses
It was rare in the mines

qs.q: What does the scholar mean by knowledge … cannot be stolen?
o: What you learn stays with you

qs.q: How does Bakari change by the end?
o: He becomes eager to learn to read
He decides to live in the desert
He wants to sell salt forever

books.title: The Salt Caravan to Timbuktu

pages.text: The ice storm knocked out the power just after dinner.
The house went dark and silent, except for the tick of the clock.
Marcus found a flashlight, but it would not turn on.
When he opened it, he saw that one battery had been put in backward.
A circuit has to be a complete loop, he remembered from science class.
Electricity flows from one end of the battery, through the bulb, and back to the other end.
He flipped the battery around and clicked the switch.
A bright beam lit up the kitchen.
His little sister, Ruby, wanted her own light.
Marcus taped a small bulb to a battery with strips of aluminum foil.
When he pressed the foil to the battery, the bulb glowed, and when he lifted it, the light went out.
You made a switch! Ruby said.
The foil is a conductor, Marcus explained.
When it touches, the circuit is closed, and when it doesn't, the circuit is open.
By the time the power came back, Ruby had named the tiny lamp Sparky.

gloss: circuit. circuit means a complete path that electricity flows through.
conductor. conductor means a material that lets electricity flow easily.
backward. backward means facing the wrong way.

qs.q: Why didn't the flashlight work at first?
What does a circuit need for electricity to flow?
Why did the bulb go out when Marcus lifted the foil?
Why is aluminum foil called a conductor?
o: It lets electricity flow through it

books.title: The Night the Lights Went Out

pages.text: Dear Papa, Norfolk is so crowded now.
Thousands of workers have come to build and fix ships at the Navy Yard, and Mama is one of them!
She learned to weld, and she wears a heavy mask and gloves.
She says the sparks look like fireworks.
Dear Papa, our class collected scrap metal for the war effort.
I gave my old roller skates.
Mrs. Hall says the metal can be melted to make ships and airplanes.
We use ration stamps now to buy sugar, meat and gasoline.
Mama says everyone must share, so there is enough for the soldiers and sailors.
Dear Papa, Grandpa and I planted a victory garden behind the house.
Growing our own food means more food can go to the troops.
I put a pressed flower from our garden in this letter.
Please come home safe.
Love, June

gloss: weld. weld means to join metal by melting it with great heat.
scrap. scrap means old pieces that can be used again.
ration. ration means a set amount each person is allowed.

qs.q: What job did Mama do at the Navy Yard?
Why did people collect scrap metal?
o: It could be melted to make ships and airplanes

qs.q: Why did families use ration stamps?
o: So there was enough for the soldiers and sailors

qs.q: How is this story told?
o: As letters from June to her father

qs.q: How does June feel about her father?
o: She misses him and worries about him

books.title: Letters from the Home Front

pages.text: Priya's model volcano had erupted perfectly every night that week.
But on the morning of the science fair, when she poured in the vinegar, nothing happened — not a single bubble.
Her friend Malik leaned closer.
Somebody sabotaged you, he whispered, glancing at the next table, where her biggest rival was setting up.
Priya shook her head.
A scientist doesn't accuse anyone without evidence.
She scooped a little of the white powder from her jar and rubbed it between her fingers.
Baking soda feels gritty, she thought, but this powder was smooth and squeaky, like cornstarch.
To be sure, she added a drop of iodine from the chemistry table.
The powder turned blue-black — a test for starch.
That afternoon, the mystery was solved at home.
Her little brother had borrowed the baking soda for cookies and refilled the jar with the closest white powder he could find.
Priya didn't win first prize, but she changed her poster.
Its new title read: Two White Powders: How Chemical Tests Reveal What Our Eyes Cannot.
The judges gave her an honorable mention, and her brother gave her a cookie.

gloss: sabotaged. sabotaged means damaged on purpose to make something fail.
rival. rival means a person you compete against.
iodine. iodine means a chemical that turns blue-black when it touches starch.
evidence. evidence means facts that show whether something is true.

qs.q: Why didn't the volcano erupt at the fair?
o: The jar held cornstarch instead of baking soda

qs.q: Which test showed the powder was starch?
o: A drop of iodine turned it blue-black

qs.q: What does A scientist doesn't accuse anyone without evidence show about Priya?
o: She relies on facts, not guesses
She is afraid of her rival

qs.q: Malik suspected the rival. Who actually caused the problem?
Which theme best fits the story?
o: Careful testing reveals the truth, even when appearances fool us

books.title: The Science Fair Mystery

pages.text: The ferry hummed across Lake Volta, and Efua leaned over the rail to watch the water.
Grandma, how deep is it here?
Grandma Adjoa was quiet for a moment.
Deep enough to cover my village, she said.
It is down there, under us.
In 1965, Ghana finished building the Akosombo Dam across the Volta River.
The water backed up behind the dam and spread over the land, creating one of the largest human-made lakes in the world.
The government said the dam would bring electricity to the whole country, and it brought a great deal, Grandma said.
Factories opened.
Cities lit up at night.
But about 80,000 people had to leave their homes.
We were resettled in a new town with houses in straight rows.
Some families never found farmland as good as what they lost.
Efua looked at the lights glowing along the shore.
So was the dam good or bad?
Grandma smiled.
Both, she said.
Big choices can help many people, but they always cost someone something, and a wise country remembers both.

gloss: ferry. ferry means a boat that carries people across water.
farmland. farmland means land used for growing crops.
resettled. resettled means moved to live in a new place.

qs.q: What created Lake Volta?
o: The Akosombo Dam backed up the Volta River

qs.q: About how many people had to leave their homes?
What does Grandma mean by Deep enough to cover my village?
o: Her old village is now underwater

qs.q: How does the author present the dam?
o: By showing both its benefits and its costs

qs.q: Which theme best fits the story?
o: Big decisions bring both benefits and costs

books.title: When the River Became a Lake

pages.text: The student council had one week to decide: should students be allowed to use phones at lunch?
Jordan, the council president, had never seen the eighth grade so divided.
At the first meeting, everyone shouted opinions.
Nobody listened, and nothing was decided.
Jordan tried something new.
Each side would present a claim, two pieces of evidence, and an answer to the other side's strongest point.
The yes side shared a survey: 64 percent of students said they used phones to contact parents about rides.
The no side cited a study from another school, where students reported talking with friends more after phones were put away at lunch.
Then the two sides did something surprising.
They looked for common ground.
Both wanted students to be safe and to have real conversations.
The council voted on a compromise: phones stay in backpacks during lunch, but students may use them in the front office to contact family.
It passed 9 to 2.
Afterward, Jordan wrote in the council notebook: Loud voices don't decide things.
Good reasons do.

gloss: divided. divided means split into groups that disagree.
evidence. evidence means facts that support a claim.
cited. cited means named as proof.
compromise. compromise means an agreement where each side gives up something.

qs.q: Why did the first meeting fail?
Which evidence did the yes side use?
What did the council decide?
o: Phones stay in backpacks at lunch, but students can use them in the office to contact family

qs.q: Why was finding common ground important?
o: It helped both sides agree on shared goals
It let one side win completely

qs.q: Which theme best fits the story?
o: Good reasons matter more than loud voices

books.title: The Vote on Phones

lessons.g4_place: Each place is worth 10 times the place to its right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, hundred-thousands. To round, look at the digit just to the RIGHT of the place you are rounding to. 5 or more rounds up; 4 or less stays. To compare big numbers, line them up and compare from the LEFT, one place at a time.
lessons.g4_frac: The bottom number (denominator) tells how many equal parts make a whole. The top (numerator) tells how many parts you have. Equivalent fractions name the same amount: multiply or divide the top AND bottom by the same number. Same bottom? Bigger top is bigger. Same top? The smaller bottom means bigger pieces.
lessons.g4_dec: After the decimal point come tenths, then hundredths. 0.7 = 7 tenths, 0.07 = 7 hundredths. To compare decimals, line up the decimal points and compare from the left. Adding a zero at the end (0.5 = 0.50) does not change the value.
lessons.g4_ops: Multiply one digit at a time, starting with the ones. Carry when a product is 10 or more. Division asks how many equal groups? Anything left over is the remainder, and it must be smaller than the divisor. Word problems: each or equal groups usually means multiply; share equally means divide.
lessons.g4_fracops: To add or subtract fractions with the SAME denominator, work only with the numerators. The denominator stays the same. For decimals, line up the decimal points first, then add or subtract like whole numbers.
lessons.g4_area: Perimeter is the distance AROUND a shape: add all the sides. Area is the space INSIDE: for a rectangle, length × width, in square units (cm², ft²). Missing side? Work backwards: width = area ÷ length.
lessons.g4_measure: Going from a BIG unit to a SMALL unit (feet → inches), multiply. Going small to big, divide. Key facts: 1 ft = 12 in · 1 yd = 3 ft · 1 m = 100 cm · 1 lb = 16 oz · 1 gal = 4 qt · 1 hr = 60 min.
lessons.g4_time: Add the hours first, then the minutes. If the minutes reach 60, trade them for 1 more hour. To find a start time, work backwards from the end time.
lessons.g4_angle: A right angle is exactly 90° (a square corner). Acute is less than 90°. Obtuse is between 90° and 180°. A line goes on forever both ways, a ray has one endpoint, a segment has two endpoints.
lessons.g4_shape: Triangles by sides: equilateral (3 equal), isosceles (2 equal), scalene (none equal). The 3 angles always add to 180°. A square has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles. A rectangle has 4 right angles. A rhombus has 4 equal sides. A trapezoid has exactly one pair of parallel sides.
lessons.g4_prob: Probability = the number of ways you want ÷ the total number of outcomes. Certain always happens, impossible never happens, likely happens more often than not.
lessons.g4_data: Read the title and the labels first. Then find the bar or point you need. How many more means subtract. Total means add. The average (mean) is the total ÷ how many numbers.
lessons.g4_pattern: Find the rule by checking what happens from one number to the next: add, subtract, or multiply? Check your rule on EVERY pair before using it to find the next number.
lessons.g4_eq: An equation is balanced like a scale. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other. Undo with the opposite: + is undone by −, × is undone by ÷.
lessons.g4_vocab: Use context clues: the words and sentences around an unknown word often explain it. Look for an example, a synonym, an opposite, or a description nearby.
lessons.g4_fiction: Theme is the lesson or message of a story. Ask: what did the character learn? To infer, combine clues from the text with what you already know. The answer is not written directly. Go back to the passage and find the sentence that proves your answer.
lessons.g4_nonfic: The main idea is what the WHOLE passage is mostly about, not just one detail. A fact can be proven; an opinion is what someone thinks or feels. Signal words show structure: first/next/finally (sequence), but/however (contrast), because/so (cause and effect).
lessons.g4_force: A force is a push or a pull. Bigger force means bigger change in motion; heavier objects need more force. Friction is a force that slows moving objects down.
lessons.g4_elec: Electricity needs a complete, closed loop (a circuit) to flow. Conductors (metals) let electricity flow; insulators (rubber, plastic, wood) block it.
lessons.g4_plants: Photosynthesis: plants use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to make sugar (food) and give off oxygen. Roots take in water, the stem carries it, leaves make food, and flowers make seeds. Animals have structures that help them survive: a bird's beak fits its food, thick fur keeps out cold, and webbed feet help with swimming.
lessons.g4_eco: Every food chain starts with a producer (a plant) that gets energy from the sun. Herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat animals, omnivores eat both. Adaptations help living things survive.
lessons.g4_weather: The water cycle: evaporation (liquid → vapor), condensation (vapor → clouds), precipitation (rain, snow). Weather is what happens today; climate is the pattern over many years.
lessons.g4_space: Earth spins on its axis once a day (day and night) and orbits the sun once a year. Seasons come from Earth's tilt. The moon reflects light from the sun.
lessons.g4_sentence: A complete sentence needs a subject (who or what) and a predicate (what they do). Start with the naming part, then the action, then the details (where, when, how).
lessons.g4_edit: Every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with punctuation. Capitalize names, days, months, and the word I. Use commas between items in a list. Match the verb to the subject: one dog runs, two dogs run.
lessons.g6_fdp: Fractions, decimals, and percents are three ways to write the same amount: ½ = 0.5 = 50%. Percent means out of 100. Decimal → percent: move the point 2 places right. To find a percent of a number, change the percent to a decimal and multiply.
lessons.g6_intns: Integers are whole numbers and their opposites: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …. On a number line, numbers get bigger as you move right. −8 is LESS than −2. Absolute value |x| is the distance from 0, so it is never negative: |−7| = 7.
lessons.g6_exp: An exponent tells how many times to multiply the base by itself: 3⁴ = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81. A perfect square is a whole number times itself: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100… A square root undoes squaring: √49 = 7 because 7 × 7 = 49.
lessons.g6_ops: Multiply fractions straight across: tops × tops, bottoms × bottoms. Simplify at the end. Divide fractions with Keep–Change–Flip: keep the first, change ÷ to ×, flip the second. Decimals: multiply like whole numbers, then count the decimal places in both numbers.
lessons.g6_int: Adding: same signs → add and keep the sign. Different signs → subtract and keep the sign of the number farther from 0. Subtracting a negative is the same as adding: 5 − (−3) = 5 + 3. Multiplying or dividing: same signs → positive. Different signs → negative.
lessons.g6_circle: The radius goes from the center to the edge. The diameter goes all the way across: d = 2 × r. Circumference (distance around) = π × d. Area (space inside) = π × r × r. Use π ≈ 3.14. Square the radius BEFORE multiplying by π.
lessons.g6_geo: Parallelogram area = base × height (use the straight-up height, not the slanted side). Triangle area = ½ × base × height, because a triangle is half of a parallelogram. Area is in square units (cm²); perimeter is in plain units (cm).
lessons.g6_coord: An ordered pair (x, y): x tells how far left/right, y tells how far up/down. Quadrant I is (+,+), II is (−,+), III is (−,−), IV is (+,−). They go counterclockwise. Reflect over the x-axis: change the sign of y. Over the y-axis: change the sign of x.
lessons.g6_congr: Congruent figures have exactly the same size AND shape. Congruent segments have equal lengths; congruent angles have equal measures.
lessons.g6_circgraph: A circle graph shows parts of a whole. All the slices add up to 100%. To find how many, multiply the percent (as a decimal) by the total.
lessons.g6_stat: Mean = add all the values and divide by how many there are. It is the balance point of the data. Median = middle value when sorted. Mode = most common. Range = greatest − least. An outlier is far from the rest. It pulls the mean much more than the median.
lessons.g6_ratio: A ratio compares two quantities: 3 to 5, 3:5, or 3/5. Order matters! Equivalent ratios come from multiplying or dividing BOTH parts by the same number. In a ratio table, every column is the same ratio scaled up or down.
lessons.g6_prop: A unit rate is the amount for ONE: divide the total by the number of units. In a proportional relationship, the ratio stays the same. Find the scale factor and use it on both parts.
lessons.g6_eq: A variable (like x) stands for an unknown number. The number in front of it is the coefficient. Solve one-step equations by doing the opposite operation to BOTH sides: x + 4 = 10 → x = 6. Check by putting your answer back into the equation.
lessons.g6_ineq: > greater than · < less than · ≥ at least · ≤ at most. An inequality has many solutions. On a number line, an open circle means the number is NOT included; a closed circle means it is.
lessons.g6_pemdas: Order of operations: Parentheses, Exponents, Multiply/Divide (left to right), Add/Subtract (left to right).
lessons.g6_vocab: Use context clues, roots, and affixes. un- means not, -ful means full of, bio means life. Connotation is the feeling a word carries: thrifty sounds positive, stingy sounds negative.
lessons.g6_fiction: Theme is a universal message; it is shown through what characters do and learn. Characterization: what a character says, does, thinks, and how others react reveals who they are. Irony is when what happens is the opposite of what you expect.
lessons.g6_nonfic: Find the author's claim, then the evidence used to support it. Author's purpose: to inform, persuade, or entertain. Ask why the author wrote it. The best evidence directly proves the claim; it is not just related to the topic.
lessons.g6_energy: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. Potential energy is stored; kinetic energy is motion. Most energy changes also give off some heat.
lessons.g6_solar: Earth rotates once a day (day and night) and revolves around the sun once a year. Moon phases come from how much of the moon's lit side we see. Seasons come from Earth's tilt.
lessons.g6_eco: Energy flows from the sun to producers, then to consumers, then to decomposers. Relationships: mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits, one unaffected), parasitism (one benefits, one harmed).
lessons.g6_atmo: Air moves from high pressure to low pressure, which makes wind. Fronts: a cold front often brings storms and cooler air. Weather happens in the lowest layer, the troposphere.
lessons.g6_resource: Renewable resources (sun, wind, water) are replaced naturally. Nonrenewable ones (oil, coal, gas) run out. Sustainable use means meeting today's needs while leaving enough for the future.
lessons.g6_race: R — Restate the question. A — Answer it directly. C — Cite evidence from the text. E — Explain how the evidence proves your answer.
lessons.g6_edit: Subject–verb agreement: Neither of the boys WAS (neither is singular). Commonly confused: its/it's, your/you're, fewer (countable) / less (not countable). Set off extra information with commas on BOTH sides.
lessons.vs1: Virginia has five regions. From the coast going west: Coastal Plain, Piedmont, Blue Ridge Mountains, Valley and Ridge, Appalachian Plateau. The Fall Line is where rivers drop to the Coastal Plain. Ships stopped there, so cities like Richmond grew. Neighbors: Maryland, West Virginia, Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Washington, D.C.
lessons.vs2: Three main language groups: Algonquian (Coastal Plain, like the Powhatan), Siouan (Piedmont, like the Monacan), and Iroquoian (southwest, like the Cherokee). Artifacts from sites such as Werowocomoco tell us how people lived. Indigenous nations are part of Virginia today, not only the past.
lessons.vs3: 1607: Jamestown, the first permanent English settlement, was founded by the Virginia Company to make money. Hardships: disease, bad water, hunger (the Starving Time). Tobacco and help from the Powhatan helped it survive. 1619: the first General Assembly met, the first recorded Africans arrived, and women were recruited to build families.
lessons.vs4: Tobacco was the main cash crop. People often bartered instead of using money. Indentured servants worked for a set time. Enslaved people were held for life. The capital moved from Jamestown to Williamsburg after a fire.
lessons.vs5: Colonists objected to taxation without representation. Virginians: Patrick Henry (speeches), Thomas Jefferson (Declaration), George Washington (army), James Armistead Lafayette (spy). The British surrendered at Yorktown in 1781. The capital moved to Richmond during the war.
lessons.vs6: James Madison is the Father of the Constitution. George Mason's Declaration of Rights shaped the Bill of Rights. Three branches: legislative makes laws, executive carries them out, judicial decides what they mean. Nat Turner's Rebellion (1831) led to harsher laws against Black Virginians.
lessons.vs7: Slavery was the main cause of the Civil War. Virginia seceded, and West Virginia split away to stay in the Union. Battles in Virginia: First Manassas, Fredericksburg, Chancellorsville, Petersburg. The war ended at Appomattox Court House. People: Robert E. Lee, Stonewall Jackson, William Harvey Carney, Harriet Tubman.
lessons.vs8: 13th Amendment: ended slavery. 14th: citizenship and equal protection. 15th: voting regardless of race. Freedmen's Schools gave education to formerly enslaved people. Plessy v. Ferguson allowed separate but equal, and Jim Crow laws enforced segregation.
lessons.vs9: After the Civil War, railroads connected cities and carried coal and goods. Factories created jobs, so many Virginians moved from rural farms to urban cities.
lessons.vs10: World War I: Woodrow Wilson (born in Staunton) was president. Richard E. Byrd explored polar regions. World War II and after: Lewis Chesty Puller served bravely. George C. Marshall's plan rebuilt Europe.
lessons.vs11: Barbara Johns led a 1951 student strike that became part of Brown v. Board of Education (1954). Massive Resistance was a plan to block desegregation. Prince Edward County closed its schools. L. Douglas Wilder was elected in 1989 as the first African American governor of a U.S. state.
lessons.vs12: Eight presidents were born in Virginia: Washington, Jefferson, Madison, Monroe, W. H. Harrison, Tyler, Taylor, and Wilson. That is why Virginia is called the Mother of Presidents.
lessons.vs13: Virginia's economy includes farming, seafood, coal, tourism, technology, ports, and the military. Exports are goods sold to other countries.
lessons.vs_sk: Maps: the compass rose shows directions, the legend explains symbols, and the scale shows real distance. Timelines: earlier events are on the left. Subtract years to find how long between events. Primary sources were made by people who were there. Secondary sources were made later.
lessons.us1: The Homestead Act (1862) and the Transcontinental Railroad (1869) drew settlers west. Barbed wire, steel plows, and windmills helped farmers on the Great Plains. Indigenous Peoples lost land and were forced onto reservations.
lessons.us2: Lincoln was assassinated in 1865. The Freedmen's Bureau helped formerly enslaved people. The 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments expanded freedom, citizenship, and voting rights. Reconstruction ended after the 1876 election. Jim Crow laws followed; leaders like Ida B. Wells and W.E.B. Du Bois fought back.
lessons.us3: Inventors like Edison and Bell, and businesses like Carnegie Steel, changed daily life. Immigrants arrived through Ellis Island and Angel Island. The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) banned most Chinese immigration. Cities grew fast, and settlement houses like Hull House helped newcomers.
lessons.us4: The Spanish-American War (1898) gave the U.S. Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines. Theodore Roosevelt: Panama Canal and national parks. The U.S. entered World War I in 1917. Afterward, the League of Nations failed to keep peace.
lessons.us5: Great Migration: African Americans moved north for jobs and freedom from Jim Crow. 1920s: women won the vote (19th Amendment), Prohibition, the Harlem Renaissance. 1929 crash → Great Depression and Dust Bowl → FDR's New Deal.
lessons.us6: Appeasement failed to stop Hitler. Pearl Harbor (1941) brought the U.S. into the war. Turning points: Midway (Pacific) and D-Day (Europe). Home front: rationing, women in factories, war bonds. The Holocaust was the murder of six million Jews and millions of others.
lessons.us7: After WWII: the United Nations, NATO, and the Marshall Plan. The Cold War was a struggle between democracy (U.S.) and communism (Soviet Union). After 9/11 (2001), the U.S. created the Department of Homeland Security.
lessons.us8: Civil rights: Brown v. Board (1954), the Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955), the Civil Rights Act (1964). Apollo 11 (1969), Watergate (1974), the EPA (1970), and the Americans with Disabilities Act (1990).
lessons.us_sk: Primary sources come from people who were there. Compare sources and think about point of view. Cause comes before effect. Facts can be proven; opinions cannot.
lessons.g7_ns1: Scientific notation writes a number as a factor from 1 to less than 10 times a power of 10, like 4.5 × 10⁴. Negative exponents mean small numbers: 10⁻³ = 1 ÷ 1,000 = 0.001. Compare numbers in scientific notation by looking at the exponents first.
lessons.g7_ns2: Change fractions and percents to decimals to compare them. On a number line, numbers increase to the right. −0.8 is less than −0.75. Absolute value is distance from zero, so it is never negative.
lessons.g7_ns3: A perfect square is a whole number times itself, like 196 = 14 × 14. The square root undoes squaring: √196 = 14.
lessons.g7_ce1: Read the problem, decide the operations, then solve step by step. Estimate first so you can check whether your answer makes sense.
lessons.g7_ce2: Percent means out of 100. 20% of 50 = 0.20 × 50 = 10. Discount: subtract from the price. Tax and tip: add to the price. A unit rate compares to 1, like miles per hour.
lessons.g7_mg1: Volume of a cylinder: V = πr²h. Surface area of a rectangular prism: SA = 2lw + 2lh + 2wh. Surface area of a cylinder: SA = 2πr² + 2πrh.
lessons.g7_mg2: Similar figures have the same shape; corresponding sides are proportional. The scale factor is new length ÷ original length.
lessons.g7_mg3: The angles of any quadrilateral add to 360°. Square ⊂ rectangle and rhombus ⊂ parallelogram. A trapezoid has exactly one pair of parallel sides.
lessons.g7_mg4: A dilation with the origin as center multiplies each coordinate by the scale factor. Scale factor > 1 enlarges; between 0 and 1 shrinks.
lessons.g7_ps1: Theoretical probability = favorable outcomes ÷ total outcomes. Experimental probability uses actual results. More trials usually bring it closer to the theoretical value.
lessons.g7_ps2: A histogram groups data into equal intervals. The height of each bar is how many values fall in that interval.
lessons.g7_pfa1: A proportional relationship can be written y = mx. The graph is a straight line through (0, 0). The slope m is the unit rate: change in y ÷ change in x.
lessons.g7_pfa2: Combine like terms: 3x + 5x = 8x. Distributive property: a(b + c) = ab + ac.
lessons.g7_pfa3: Undo operations in reverse order: first add or subtract, then multiply or divide. Check your answer by substituting it back in.
lessons.g7_pfa4: Solve inequalities like equations. On a number line, use an open circle for < or > and a closed circle for ≤ or ≥.
lessons.g8_ns1: Estimate a square root by finding the perfect squares on either side: √50 is between 7 and 8. Every positive number has two square roots, one positive and one negative.
lessons.g8_ns2: Natural ⊂ whole ⊂ integers ⊂ rational ⊂ real numbers. Irrational numbers, like π and √2, are non-repeating, non-ending decimals.
lessons.g8_ce1: Percent change = amount of change ÷ original amount. Simple interest: I = P × r × t.
lessons.g8_mg1: Vertical angles are congruent. Supplementary angles add to 180°. Complementary angles add to 90°.
lessons.g8_mg2: Volume of a cone: V = ⅓πr²h. Volume of a pyramid: V = ⅓Bh. Surface area of a square pyramid = base + 4 triangles.
lessons.g8_mg3: Translation: slide every point the same distance. Reflect over the x-axis: (x, y) → (x, −y). Over the y-axis: (x, y) → (−x, y).
lessons.g8_mg4: In a right triangle, a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse. Use it to find a missing side or to check whether a triangle is a right triangle.
lessons.g8_mg5: Split a composite figure into rectangles, triangles, and circle parts. Add the parts (or subtract a cut-out part).
lessons.g8_ps1: Independent events: multiply the probabilities. Dependent events: after the first pick, update the numbers before multiplying.
lessons.g8_ps2: A boxplot shows the minimum, Q1, median, Q3, and maximum. The interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 − Q1 and holds the middle 50% of the data.
lessons.g8_ps3: A scatterplot shows how two variables relate: positive, negative, or no relationship. A line of best fit can be used to make predictions.
lessons.g8_pfa1: Distribute first, then combine like terms. Watch negative signs when distributing.
lessons.g8_pfa2: A function pairs each input with exactly one output. Domain = all inputs (x). Range = all outputs (y).
lessons.g8_pfa3: In y = mx + b, m is the slope and b is the y-intercept. Slope = (y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁).
lessons.g8_pfa4: Move variable terms to one side and numbers to the other. Keep both sides balanced: do the same thing to each side.
lessons.g8_pfa5: Solve like an equation. When you multiply or divide by a negative number, flip the inequality sign.
lessons.r7_vocab: Use context clues around an unknown word. Roots and affixes help: trans- = across, aud = hear. Connotation is the feeling a word gives: thrifty (positive) vs. stingy (negative).
lessons.r7_fiction: Conflict can be internal (inside a character) or external. Theme is the lesson or message about life. Point of view: first person uses I; third person uses he or she.
lessons.r7_nonfic: Main idea: what the whole passage is mostly about. Text structures: sequence, cause and effect, compare and contrast, problem and solution. A claim is an opinion supported by evidence.
lessons.r8_vocab: Greek and Latin roots unlock many words: chron = time, mal- = bad. Figurative language says something non-literally.
lessons.r8_fiction: Foreshadowing hints at future events. Irony is the difference between what is expected and what happens. Indirect characterization shows character through actions and words.
lessons.r8_nonfic: Strong arguments use relevant evidence and address counterclaims. Check sources for reliability. Persuasive techniques include bandwagon, expert opinion, and statistics.
lessons.w7_write: A thesis states your main claim. Use transitions to connect ideas: however, therefore, for example.
lessons.w7_edit: Indefinite pronouns like each and neither are singular. Place modifiers next to the word they describe.
lessons.w8_write: Address a counterclaim, then explain why your claim is stronger. Cite sources to avoid plagiarism.
lessons.w8_edit: Use active voice for clear writing. Keep items in a list parallel. Use were for imagined situations: If I were…
lessons.ls2: Cell theory: all living things are made of cells, cells are the basic unit of life, and cells come from cells. Plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts; animal cells do not. Mitosis makes identical cells for growth and repair.
lessons.ls3: Levels: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism. Classification: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
lessons.ls4: Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water + light → glucose + oxygen. Cellular respiration releases energy from glucose.
lessons.ls5: Biotic = living; abiotic = nonliving. Only about 10% of energy passes to the next level of an energy pyramid. Decomposers recycle nutrients.
lessons.ls6: Symbiosis: mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits, one unaffected), parasitism (one harmed). Limited resources lead to competition and set the carrying capacity.
lessons.ls7: Structural adaptations are body features; behavioral adaptations are actions. Camouflage and mimicry help organisms avoid predators.
lessons.ls10: DNA carries genetic information. Dominant alleles (capital letters) hide recessive alleles. Punnett squares predict offspring.
lessons.ls11: Fossils show how life has changed over time. Natural selection: organisms with helpful traits survive and reproduce.
lessons.ps2: Atoms have protons (+), neutrons (0), and electrons (−). The atomic number is the number of protons.
lessons.ps3: Physical changes do not make new substances; chemical changes do. Mass is conserved in chemical reactions.
lessons.ps4: The periodic table is ordered by atomic number. Groups (columns) share similar properties. Metals are on the left.
lessons.ps5: Potential energy is stored; kinetic energy is motion. Energy changes form but is conserved. Heat moves by conduction, convection, and radiation.
lessons.ps6: Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium. Frequency affects pitch; amplitude affects loudness.
lessons.ps7: The electromagnetic spectrum goes from radio waves (long) to gamma rays (short). EM waves can travel through empty space.
lessons.ps8: Newton's laws: inertia, F = ma, and action–reaction. Speed = distance ÷ time. Work = force × distance.
lessons.ps9: Series circuits have one path; parallel circuits have several. Like poles repel; opposite poles attract.
lessons.ce1: Principles: popular sovereignty, limited government, federalism, separation of powers, checks and balances. The Constitution replaced the weak Articles of Confederation.
lessons.ce2: Legislative makes laws, executive carries them out, judicial interprets them. Checks and balances: veto, override, judicial review.
lessons.ce3: Virginia's General Assembly has the House of Delegates and the Senate. The Governor leads the executive branch for a four-year term.
lessons.ce4: Local governments get their power from the General Assembly. Local laws are called ordinances.
lessons.ce5: There are state courts and federal courts. Criminal cases involve crimes; civil cases settle private disputes.
lessons.ce6: Citizenship comes by birth or naturalization. Duties are required (obey laws, pay taxes); responsibilities are expected (vote, stay informed).
lessons.ce7: Good citizens show civility, honesty, respect, and responsibility. Community service promotes the common good.
lessons.ce8: Political parties recruit candidates and inform voters. A presidential candidate needs 270 of 538 electoral votes.
lessons.ce9: A free press informs citizens and checks government. Compare sources to spot bias.
lessons.ce11: Scarcity forces choices. Opportunity cost is the next-best choice given up. Prices are set by supply and demand in a market economy.
lessons.ce12: Government provides public goods like roads and defense. Fiscal policy = taxing and spending. Monetary policy = the Federal Reserve.
lessons.ce13: A budget plans spending and saving. Good credit means lower interest rates. Diversify to reduce risk.
lessons.wg1: Latitude measures north–south; longitude measures east–west. GIS layers data on digital maps. All flat maps distort Earth.
lessons.wg2: Resources: natural, human, and capital. Uneven resources lead countries to trade.
lessons.wg3: The Rockies are in the west; the Appalachians in the east. The St. Lawrence Seaway links the Great Lakes to the Atlantic.
lessons.wg4: The Andes run along western South America. The Amazon is the largest rainforest.
lessons.wg5: The Alps cross central Europe. Warm ocean currents give Western Europe a mild climate.
lessons.wg6: Russia is the largest country by area. The Ural Mountains divide Europe and Asia.
lessons.wg7: Savannas cover much of sub-Saharan Africa. The Sahel borders the Sahara and faces desertification.
lessons.wg8: The Nile Valley is fertile land in the desert. Oil is a key resource near the Persian Gulf.
lessons.wg9: The Himalayas include Mount Everest. Monsoons bring heavy summer rain.
lessons.wg10: Japan lies on the Ring of Fire. The Yangtze is Asia's longest river.
lessons.wg11: Most Australians live along the coasts. Low-lying Pacific Islands face rising seas.
lessons.wg12: Population density = people ÷ area. GDP per capita helps measure standard of living.
lessons.wg13: Push factors drive people away; pull factors attract them. Refugees flee war or persecution.
lessons.wg14: Culture includes language, religion, food, and customs. Cultural diffusion spreads ideas between groups.
lessons.wg15: Urbanization: people moving from rural areas to cities. Cities often grow near water for trade and transportation.
lessons.wg16: Globalization connects countries through trade and technology. Countries depend on one another to make goods.
lessons.wg17: Borders can be disputed over resources or history. Chokepoints like straits and canals control shipping.
lessons.g1_ns1: Skip count by adding the same number each time: 5, 10, 15, 20. A two-digit number is tens and ones: 47 is 4 tens and 7 ones. A penny is 1¢, a nickel is 5¢, and a dime is 10¢.
lessons.g1_ns2: Compare the tens first. If the tens are the same, compare the ones. > means greater than; < means less than.
lessons.g1_ns3: Halves: 2 equal parts. Fourths: 4 equal parts. Equal shares must be the same size.
lessons.g1_ce1: Count on to add; count back to subtract. Part + part = whole.
lessons.g1_mg1: Line things up at the same starting point to compare length. More units means longer.
lessons.g1_mg2: Triangles have 3 sides; squares and rectangles have 4. Squares and rectangles have 4 right angles.
lessons.g1_mg3: The short hand shows the hour. The long hand shows the minutes. When the long hand is on 12, it is o'clock. On 6, it is half past.
lessons.g1_ps1: Count the pictures in each row. Compare rows to see which has more.
lessons.g1_pfa1: Find the part that repeats. Growing patterns add the same amount each time.
lessons.g2_ns1: Skip count by 2s, 5s, 10s, 25s, and 100s. Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8.
lessons.g2_ns2: In 547: 5 hundreds, 4 tens, 7 ones. Expanded form: 500 + 40 + 7.
lessons.g2_ns3: The bottom number tells how many equal parts. With unit fractions, more parts means smaller pieces.
lessons.g2_ns4: Quarter 25¢, dime 10¢, nickel 5¢, penny 1¢. Count the biggest coins first.
lessons.g2_ce1: Add or subtract tens, then ones. Regroup 10 ones as 1 ten when needed.
lessons.g2_mg1: Inches measure length, pounds measure weight, cups measure liquid.
lessons.g2_mg2: Count by 5s around the clock for minutes.
lessons.g2_mg3: A line of symmetry makes two matching halves.
lessons.g2_mg4: Cubes and rectangular prisms have 6 faces, 12 edges, and 8 vertices. A sphere has no flat faces.
lessons.g2_ps1: Follow the top of each bar across to the numbers.
lessons.g2_pfa1: Find the rule: how much is added each time?
lessons.g3_ns1: Each place is 10 times the place to its right. Value = digit × place.
lessons.g3_ns2: Line up the digits and compare from the left.
lessons.g3_ns3: Same denominator: compare numerators. Same numerator: the smaller denominator is the bigger fraction. 2 1/4 = 9/4.
lessons.g3_ns4: Count up from the price to find change.
lessons.g3_ce1: Add and subtract by place value. Regroup when needed. Estimate by rounding to check your answer.
lessons.g3_ce2: Multiplication is equal groups. Division undoes multiplication.
lessons.g3_mg1: Customary: inches, feet, pounds, cups. Metric: centimeters, meters, grams, liters.
lessons.g3_mg2: Area = square units inside. Perimeter = distance around.
lessons.g3_mg3: Elapsed time is how much time passes between start and end.
lessons.g3_mg4: Polygons are closed shapes with straight sides. Triangle 3, quadrilateral 4, pentagon 5, hexagon 6, octagon 8.
lessons.g3_ps1: Read each bar carefully, then add or subtract.
lessons.g3_pfa1: Decide whether the pattern grows or shrinks, and by how much.
lessons.r1_ffr: Rhyming words end with the same sound. Say each sound slowly, then blend.
lessons.r1_rv: Opposites mean very different things: hot and cold. Compound words are two words put together.
lessons.r1_rl: Characters are who the story is about. The setting is where and when. Retell the beginning, middle, and end.
lessons.r1_ri: The topic is what the text is mostly about. Titles and captions give clues.
lessons.r2_ffr: A silent e makes the vowel say its name. Clap to count syllables.
lessons.r2_rv: un- means not; re- means again. Synonyms mean the same; antonyms mean the opposite.
lessons.r2_rl: The lesson is what a character learns. Use clues to predict what happens next.
lessons.r2_ri: The main idea is the big point. Headings, glossaries, and captions help readers.
lessons.r3_ffr: Divide words into syllables to read them. Suffixes like -ful and -less change meaning.
lessons.r3_rv: Homophones sound the same but have different meanings. Idioms do not mean exactly what the words say.
lessons.r3_rl: Characters can change from the beginning to the end. A fable teaches a moral.
lessons.r3_ri: Find the main idea and the details that support it. Text structure: sequence, cause and effect, compare.
lessons.w1_w: A sentence tells a complete thought. Telling sentences end with a period.
lessons.w1_lu: Begin sentences and names with capital letters. Questions end with a question mark.
lessons.w2_w: Stories have a beginning, middle, and end. Use order words: first, next, then, last.
lessons.w2_lu: Contractions use an apostrophe for missing letters. Add -s or -es to make plurals.
lessons.w3_w: A paragraph has a topic sentence, details, and a closing sentence.
lessons.w3_lu: Use commas in a list. Use 's to show ownership.
lessons.sc1_2: Pushes and pulls make things move. Sound is made by vibrations.
lessons.sc1_3: Objects are made of materials like wood, metal, glass, and cloth.
lessons.sc1_4: Plants need water, light, air, and space. Roots, stems, and leaves each have a job.
lessons.sc1_5: Animals need food, water, air, and shelter.
lessons.sc1_6: The sun gives Earth light and heat. Shadows form when light is blocked.
lessons.sc1_7: Seasons change temperature, plants, and animals.
lessons.sc1_8: Reduce, reuse, and recycle to save resources.
lessons.sc2_2: Forces push or pull. Magnets attract iron and steel; like poles repel.
lessons.sc2_3: Matter can be a solid, liquid, or gas. Heating and cooling change states.
lessons.sc2_4: Living things grow and change in life cycles.
lessons.sc2_5: A habitat provides food, water, and shelter.
lessons.sc2_6: Thermometers, rain gauges, and weather vanes measure weather.
lessons.sc2_7: Weather and seasons change land and living things.
lessons.sc2_8: Plants give us food, wood, cloth, and oxygen.
lessons.sc3_2: Bigger forces cause bigger changes in motion. Balanced forces do not change motion.
lessons.sc3_3: Some solids dissolve in water, especially warm water.
lessons.sc3_4: Physical adaptations are body parts; behavioral adaptations are actions.
lessons.sc3_5: Food chains start with the sun and producers.
lessons.sc3_6: Topsoil has humus and nutrients. Clay holds water; sand drains quickly.
lessons.sc3_8: Natural events and people can change ecosystems.
lessons.h1_1: Good citizens follow rules, take turns, and help others.
lessons.h1_3: The flag and bald eagle are American symbols.
lessons.h1_4: Werowocomoco was Chief Powhatan's town. Jamestown was settled in 1607.
lessons.h1_5: Many Virginians helped shape our state and nation.
lessons.h1_6: Maps use keys and compass roses.
lessons.h1_8: Needs are required to live; wants are nice to have. Goods are things; services are work done for others.
lessons.h2_4: Richmond is Virginia's capital; Washington, D.C., is the nation's capital.
lessons.h2_5: Indigenous peoples used the resources of their regions.
lessons.h2_6: Explorers came from Spain, England, and France.
lessons.h2_8: The Declaration of Independence was adopted in 1776.
lessons.h2_9: The Louisiana Purchase doubled the size of the U.S.
lessons.h2_10: Changemakers invented, explored, and worked for fairness.
lessons.h2_11: Learn the oceans, rivers, and mountains of the U.S.
lessons.h2_13: Resources are natural, human, or capital. Scarcity means we must make choices.
lessons.h3_5: China: Great Wall, silk, paper, the Huang He.
lessons.h3_6: Greece: democracy, the Olympics, the Parthenon.
lessons.h3_7: Rome: republic, roads, aqueducts, the Colosseum.
lessons.h3_8: Mali: Mansa Musa, Timbuktu, gold and salt.
lessons.h3_10: Specialization and trade help people get what they need.
lessons.g5_ns1: Fractions and decimals can name the same amount: 1/4 = 0.25, 3/5 = 0.6. To compare, change both to decimals (or both to fractions with the same denominator). Line up the decimal points and compare place by place.
lessons.g5_ns2: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. A composite number has more than two factors. Prime factorization writes a number as a product of primes: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3.
lessons.g5_ce1: Read carefully: which operation does each step need? Estimate first, then check that your answer is reasonable. In division, decide what to do with the remainder.
lessons.g5_ce2: Same denominators: add or subtract the numerators. Unlike denominators: find a common denominator first. Whole number × fraction: multiply the whole number by the numerator.
lessons.g5_ce3: Line up decimal points to add or subtract. When multiplying, count the decimal places in the factors. When dividing, place the decimal point straight up in the quotient.
lessons.g5_ce4: Order of operations: Parentheses, then multiply and divide left to right, then add and subtract left to right.
lessons.g5_mg1: 1 km = 1,000 m; 1 m = 100 cm; 1 cm = 10 mm. 1 kg = 1,000 g; 1 L = 1,000 mL. To change a larger unit to a smaller one, multiply.
lessons.g5_mg2: Perimeter is the distance around. Area is square units inside. Area of a right triangle = ½ × base × height. Volume of a rectangular prism = length × width × height (cubic units).
lessons.g5_mg3: Acute < 90°, right = 90°, obtuse > 90°. The angles of a triangle add to 180°. Triangles by sides: equilateral, isosceles, scalene.
lessons.g5_ps1: In a stem-and-leaf plot, the stem is the tens and the leaf is the ones: 3 | 7 means 37. In a line plot, each X stands for one data value.
lessons.g5_ps2: Mean: add and divide. Median: middle value in order. Mode: most often. Range: greatest − least.
lessons.g5_ps3: A sample space lists every possible outcome. Fundamental Counting Principle: multiply the number of choices at each step.
lessons.g5_pfa1: Find the rule: how does each term change? Patterns can use whole numbers, fractions, or decimals.
lessons.g5_pfa2: A variable is a letter that stands for an unknown number. Write an equation to match the story, then solve.
lessons.r5_rv: Use roots and affixes: bio = life, -ology = study of. Context clues: definitions, examples, and contrasts nearby. Figurative language: similes, metaphors, personification, idioms.
lessons.r5_rl: Theme is the message about life, shown through what characters do and learn. Point of view: first person (I) or third person (he, she, they).
lessons.r5_ri: The main idea is supported by key details. Text structures: sequence, compare/contrast, cause/effect, problem/solution.
lessons.w5_w: Opinion writing: state a claim and give reasons with evidence. Narratives use dialogue, description, and a clear sequence. Informative writing groups related facts under topics.
lessons.w5_lu: Use commas after introductory words and in a series. Make subjects and verbs agree. Use quotation marks around exact words.
lessons.sc5_2: Energy forms include mechanical, sound, light, electrical, chemical, and thermal. Energy can change from one form to another.
lessons.sc5_3: A force is a push or pull. More mass needs more force to move the same amount. Moving objects have kinetic energy.
lessons.sc5_4: Current electricity flows in a closed circuit. Static electricity is a buildup of charge. An electromagnet is a coil of wire around iron with current flowing.
lessons.sc5_5: Sound is made by vibrations and travels as waves. Sound travels fastest through solids and cannot travel through empty space. Pitch depends on frequency; volume depends on amplitude.
lessons.sc5_6: Light travels in straight lines as waves. Light can be reflected, refracted, or absorbed. White light is made of the visible spectrum: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
lessons.sc5_7: All matter is made of atoms. Matter can be a solid, liquid, or gas. Mixtures can be separated; solutions are mixtures where one substance dissolves.
lessons.sc5_8: The rock cycle: igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic. Earth's plates move slowly, causing earthquakes and volcanoes. Weathering breaks rock; erosion moves it.
lessons.sc5_9: Renewable resources can be replaced; nonrenewable ones run out. Conserving energy saves resources and money.
lessons.usi1: North America has coastal plains, mountains, plateaus, and a large interior plain. Major waters: the Mississippi River, the Great Lakes, the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
lessons.usi2: Archaeologists study artifacts to learn about the past. Indigenous Peoples adapted to their environments across North America.
lessons.usi3: Spain, France, Portugal, and England explored the Americas for wealth, land, and faith. Exploration brought both cooperation and conflict.
lessons.usi4: West African kingdoms like Ghana, Mali, and Songhai grew rich from trade. Millions of Africans were forced across the Atlantic in the Transatlantic Slave Trade.
lessons.usi5: New England, the Mid-Atlantic, and the Southern colonies had different economies. Geography shaped how people lived and worked.
lessons.usi6: Taxes without representation angered colonists. The Declaration of Independence (1776) explained why the colonies broke away. The war ended with victory at Yorktown (1781).
lessons.usi7: The Articles of Confederation created a weak national government. The Constitution (1787) set up three branches. The first five presidents: Washington, Adams, Jefferson, Madison, Monroe.
lessons.usi8: The Louisiana Purchase (1803) doubled the nation's size. Reform movements worked to end slavery and gain women's rights.
lessons.usi9: Disagreements over slavery and states' rights led to the Civil War (1861–1865). Lincoln led the Union; the war ended at Appomattox in 1865.
lessons.usi_sk: Primary sources come from the time; secondary sources come later. Use timelines to sequence events.
lessons.g4_cmp: Line the numbers up by place value. Start at the greatest place and compare digit by digit. The first place where the digits differ decides which number is greater. > means greater than, < means less than. The open side faces the bigger number.
lessons.g4_fdrel: Tenths and hundredths can be written two ways: 7/10 = 0.7 and 23/100 = 0.23. Halves, fourths and fifths: change them to tenths or hundredths first. 1/2 = 5/10 = 0.5, 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25, 1/5 = 2/10 = 0.2. Read 0.45 as forty-five hundredths — that is 45/100.
lessons.g4_addsub: Line up the digits by place value, then add or subtract starting with the ones. Regroup when you need to: 10 ones make 1 ten, 10 tens make 1 hundred. Estimate first by rounding. If your exact answer is far from the estimate, check your work.
lessons.g4_decops: Line up the decimal points before you add or subtract. Fill empty places with zeros: 4.5 is the same as 4.500. Bring the decimal point straight down into your answer.
lessons.g4_solid: Plane figures are flat (square, rectangle, triangle, circle). Solid figures take up space (cube, prism, pyramid, cylinder, cone, sphere). A face is a flat surface, an edge is where two faces meet, and a vertex is a corner where edges meet. A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. A square pyramid has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices.
lessons.g4_esm: Earth spins (rotates) on its axis once every 24 hours. That makes day and night. Earth travels (revolves) around the sun once a year, about 365 days. Its tilted axis causes the seasons. The moon does not make light; it reflects sunlight. Its phases repeat about every 29½ days, and its gravity causes most of the ocean's tides.
lessons.g4_ocean: The ocean floor has a continental shelf, a continental slope, a wide abyssal plain, ridges and deep trenches. Ocean water is salty. Deeper water is colder, darker, and under more pressure. Tiny plankton are the base of ocean food webs. Phytoplankton make food from sunlight and give off much of Earth's oxygen.
lessons.g4_vares: Virginia's natural resources include water, forests, soil, minerals, coal, and land for farming. Most of Virginia's land drains into the Chesapeake Bay, the largest estuary in the United States. Renewable resources (trees, water, sunlight) can be replaced; nonrenewable ones (coal, oil) cannot. Conserve both.
lessons.g6_esm: Seasons happen because Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5° as it orbits the sun. A solar eclipse happens when the moon passes between the sun and Earth; a lunar eclipse when Earth is between the sun and the moon. Spring tides (biggest range) happen at new and full moon, when the sun and moon line up; neap tides happen at the quarter moons.
lessons.g6_atoms: Atoms are made of protons (+) and neutrons (no charge) in the nucleus, with electrons (−) around it. An element is made of only one kind of atom (O, H, Fe). A compound is two or more elements chemically joined (H₂O, CO₂). In a chemical reaction, reactants become products. Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed.
lessons.g6_water: Water dissolves so many things that it is called the universal solvent. Water has a high specific heat: it heats up and cools down slowly, which keeps coastal climates mild. Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats. Water molecules stick together (cohesion), causing surface tension.
lessons.g6_bay: A watershed is all the land that drains into a body of water. Virginia has three major watershed systems: the Chesapeake Bay, the North Carolina sounds, and the Gulf of Mexico (through the Mississippi River system). The Chesapeake Bay is an estuary, where fresh river water mixes with salt water. Runoff with too many nutrients can cause algae blooms and low oxygen.

cases.text: Max's sneakers by the door are covered in mud. His raincoat is dripping on the floor. A soccer ball in the hall is wet and grassy. The kitchen smells like cookies. What was Max doing before he came inside?
Whiskers the cat is licking her lips. Her food bowl was full this morning. Now the bowl is empty. A ball of yarn is under the couch. What happened to the food?
Mom hides a wrapped box behind her back. Balloons are tied to Lena's chair. Everyone stops talking when Lena walks in. It is raining outside. What is probably happening?
The soil is dry and cracked. The watering can in the shed is still full. It has not rained in two weeks. A bird sings in the apple tree. Why are the tomato plants drooping?
Ana's poster has a big blue ribbon on it. She is smiling and holding a trophy. Her teacher shakes her hand. The gym lights are bright. What happened at the science fair?
Jamal's shoelaces are untied. He has toothpaste on his chin. He grabs his backpack and runs out the door. His goldfish swims in its bowl. What can you tell about Jamal?
The school bus did not come today. Dad is shoveling the driveway. Kids are building a snowman in the park. The TV says All schools closed. Grandma is reading a book. Why is there no school today?

The lab door was locked all night, and only Ms. Ortiz has a key. This morning, the window is open and the screen is torn. Small muddy paw prints lead from the window to the snack cabinet. A granola bar wrapper lies on the floor, chewed at the edges. The class hamster is asleep in its closed cage. Who most likely got into the lab?

Priya put one bean plant by a sunny window and one in a dark closet. She gave both plants the same amount of water every day. After two weeks, the window plant was tall and green. The closet plant was pale yellow and thin. Priya's brother practices piano after school. What can Priya conclude?

The letter is written with a quill pen on yellowed paper. It is dated March 1775. The writer complains about new taxes on paper and tea. He signs it, Your loving son, in Williamsburg. A museum visitor left a coffee cup beside it today. What is the best conclusion about the letter?

Coach Lee set the gold medal on top of the equipment bag before practice. Rain started halfway through practice, and everyone hurried to the bus. Devon says he saw something shiny slide into the equipment bag. The equipment bag was carried onto the bus with the balls. The bus driver honked twice. Where is the medal most likely now?

Every house on Oak Street went dark at 6:15 p.m. Houses on Maple Street, one block away, still had lights. A large branch is lying across the power line on Oak Street. The wind was very strong that evening. Someone on Maple Street was cooking spaghetti. What most likely caused the outage?

The class voted on a trip: the history museum or the zoo. Most students wrote animals! on their idea cards. The teacher handed out permission slips with a lion on them. The museum is closed for repairs that week. Lunch will be pizza. Where is the class most likely going?

Mr. Grant's newspapers have piled up on his porch for a week. His car is gone from the driveway. A neighbor is watering his plants each evening. He mentioned planning a trip to see his grandchildren. The street was repaved last month. What is the most likely explanation?
